summary.title: Build once, run on any agent: A practical guide to agent skills
summary.idea: Repeated explanations to agents get lost in chat, so capture them as versioned SKILL.md files with project config in a manifest, an independent verifier, and human checkpoints.
howItWorks: Each skill is a SKILL.md directory with one job, clear input and output, and a description of when to use it.
Project names, schemas and conventions live in a resolved manifest that every skill reads, rather than being hardcoded.
One shared skill handles platform access, picking the right adapter from the manifest, so skills don't duplicate connection logic.
A separate verifier sees the original request and diff, not the coding agent's self-assessment, and returns PASS, FAIL or PARTIAL with cited evidence.
A packaging script generates client-specific plugin files from the skills source, with a CI check mode to catch drift.
summary.stealThis: Before your next code review, add a verifier skill run in CI that gets only the original request and the diff, and must return PASS, FAIL or PARTIAL with cited evidence.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're building multi-skill workflows or want one skills source working across Claude Code, Cursor and Copilot.
summary.quote: At the center is a simple rule: self-verification is not verification.

verdict.reason: Teaches portable skill-design patterns with config snippets, all matching the card: single-job SKILL.md files, a shared manifest for project context, one shared platform-access skill, an independent PASS/FAIL/PARTIAL verifier that never sees the coder's self-assessment, and a packaging script with a CI --check mode.

summary.title: Catch Go bugs that fuzzing misses with Gemini and a constraint solver
summary.idea: Fuzzing and LLM code review both miss subtle Go bounds bugs, so the author has an agent turn the compiled assembly into Z3 constraints, then replays any solver counterexample with go test.
howItWorks: Compile the target function with -gcflags="-S -d=ssa/check_bce/debug=1" to list the bounds checks the optimizer could not remove.
Give the model both the Go source and the disassembly, and have it write a Z3 script for the path to each surviving panic trap.
Z3 answers sat with concrete bytes or unsat in milliseconds; the model's translation takes about a minute per function.
Replay each sat input through go test against the real function, so every reported crash is a verified reproducer.
Extract pure parsing and slice helpers, including their entry guards, so the solver does not invent inputs that callers would never pass.
summary.stealThis: Before your next fuzz run on a Go parser, add data = data[:len(data):len(data)] inside the Fuzz function so overruns into spare capacity panic instead of passing silently.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're building agent loops that hunt bugs and want a pattern where an unsound LLM-written model still yields hard, replayable evidence.
summary.quote: Once go test panics, you have a concrete bug reproducer regardless of whether Argon's model was sound.

verdict.reason: The page teaches a portable verification loop with real code and before/after results: an LLM translates Go source plus disassembly into Z3 constraints, and every sat counterexample is replayed through go test as a proven reproducer, alongside a one-line cap==len fuzz fix; it is narrow to Go bounds bugs.

summary.title: Cyber Chaos Monkey: Staying ahead of security threats with AI agents
summary.idea: Letting an offensive agent loose on live systems risks it breaking rules or leaking access; Shopify contains it with least privilege, proxies, and a second differently-aligned judge agent that can kill the run.
howItWorks: The executor agent runs in an unprivileged container, seeded only with ephemeral, read-only credentials written by the orchestrator.
A credential proxy swaps placeholder headers for real secrets, restricted per domain, so the agent never holds long-lived keys.
An egress proxy allowlist permits only production domains, knowledge services, model providers and approved package managers.
A judge agent on a different model reads every executor event live and calls a tool to kill the run on rule violations.
An orchestrator heartbeats both sidecars; if the judge or executor dies or times out, the pod terminates and does not restart.
summary.stealThis: Before you give an agent real credentials or autonomy, add a second agent on a different model that watches its session log and can kill it, failing closed if the judge stops responding.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're running agents against live systems and need a concrete containment design covering credentials, egress, and fail-closed oversight.
summary.quote: if the "judge" times out, crashes, or fails to adjudicate messages from the "executor," the run ends.

verdict.reason: The page teaches a transferable containment pattern: a judge agent on a different model reads the executor's full session log live and can kill the run, failing closed on timeout. It adds placeholder-header credential proxying and an egress allowlist; the design is concrete, though there's no code.

summary.title: Goal Engineering: How to Design Goals
summary.idea: Agents fail for lack of unwritten expert context, so scope each agent around a kind of job that is easy for humans to review and give feedback on, not around an object like an account.
howItWorks: Scope the agent so a human can review many similar outputs together and give feedback in one sitting.
Organise agents by job to be done (a 'motion', such as outbounding), not by entity such as one account.
Feedback on one task in a job transfers to the other tasks in that same job.
Run background context-gathering agents to assemble objective, already-written facts, and pull them in on demand.
Invest in a clear review UX, since learning from feedback is usually the bottleneck.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent design, group its work by repeatable job rather than by customer or ticket, so one batch of similar outputs can be reviewed together and the corrections reused.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're building long-running agents for subjective work like sales or marketing and want to decide how to scope them for feedback.
summary.quote: The bottleneck for agents performing is often them learning from feedback.

verdict.reason: It teaches one transferable scoping pattern, organising agents by repeatable job ('motion') rather than by entity so feedback can be batched and reused, backed by a before-and-after case study, but it has no code or detail on how feedback is captured and propagated.

summary.title: Generated Glossary
summary.idea: Agents stumble on an organisation's specialised vocabulary, so have an LLM draft a glossary from internal documents, let experts correct it, and make it available to every agent doing domain work.
howItWorks: Feed the generator internal documents, emails, chat logs and code, asking for multi-word terms and familiar words used in unfamiliar ways.
Ask for dictionary-style, concise definitions, with alternative definitions and context notes where a term is used differently.
Have domain experts review the draft, then store it in version control in a token-cheap format agents can consult.
Keep separate glossaries per bounded context rather than one standard; for large ones, load only terms and links first.
Include deprecated or forbidden terms with replacements, and use harness sensors to check code and UI text against the glossary.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent project in a jargon-heavy domain, have an LLM mine your docs and code for a draft glossary, get an expert to fix it, and commit it where agents can read it.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're running agents in a large organisation where internal jargon and overlapping definitions keep leading them astray.
summary.quote: I'd urge everyone to resist any temptation to create a single, standard, glossary - I've yet to see that work.

verdict.reason: Teaches a clear, copyable context technique: have an LLM mine org docs and code for a domain glossary, get experts to correct it, version it per bounded context, and load terms-plus-links for large ones; there are no examples or prompts, so it scores as thin.

summary.title: Your coding agent's "done" is a claim. Plan the checks between steps
summary.idea: Agents report "done" after passing their own tests, but across chained requests unnoticed failures compound; a written chain plan with checks the agent can't edit stops errors building on errors.
howItWorks: Write a table before the session: each request, what it builds on, and whether it is a foundation step.
Give every step a check the agent can't edit, such as a contract test, a SQL comparison or a hand test.
Block foundation steps from getting a successor until their check column says Pass.
Re-run earlier steps' checks at every step, since later requests often break earlier passing tests.
Feed failures back as the exact test name and error, then allow one repair round and re-check.
summary.stealThis: Before your next multi-step agent session, paste the CHAIN.md table into the ticket and ban "agent's tests pass" from the check column, naming a file, test or person instead.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're running agents through long chains of dependent requests and want benchmark evidence plus a ready-made template for gating each step.
summary.quote: The agent's own tests are not your gate.

verdict.reason: Teaches a concrete chain-plan template (CHAIN.md table with agent-uneditable checks, foundation gating, regression re-runs, named-failure feedback) grounded in benchmark evidence, though the rules are the author's inference rather than a demonstrated working setup.

summary.title: Amit Got Stuck Reviewing Agent Code: Green CI, Wrong Behaviour
summary.idea: When one agent writes both code and tests, they agree with each other and CI goes green even if the behaviour is wrong; separate sessions and a test-first reading order fix this.
howItWorks: Split work into three sessions: implement, write tests from the spec alone, and review the diff with no reasoning attached.
Read agent pull requests in a fixed order: spec, diff summary, tests, dependencies and config, error handling, then the rest.
Run mutation testing (StrykerJS) on the changed folder to check that the tests actually fail when the code is broken.
Add CI checks that flag new dependencies and any change to existing test assertions, plus a pull request size limit.
Check every new package by hand, since models invent names that attackers register (slopsquatting).
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent-written pull request is merged, have a fresh session write tests from the spec only, then run mutation testing on the changed folder to see whether those tests catch broken code.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're reviewing more agent-written pull requests than you can read closely and want a reading order and checklist that catch fluent but wrong code.
summary.quote: Consistent is not the same as correct.

verdict.reason: It teaches concrete review guardrails: a separate fresh session that writes tests from the spec, a fixed test-first PR reading order, StrykerJS mutation testing with commands, and CI flags for new dependencies and changed assertions; the story is invented, though, so there is no real before-and-after evidence.

summary.title: My coding agent said "done" 1,521 times. Half of those had nothing behind them.
summary.idea: Coding agents often claim success without a passing check behind it; a stop hook that blocks a turn from ending on a success claim unless a test, build or lint passed that turn fixes it.
howItWorks: Log each session and flag every 'done' claim: tests pass, bug fixed, build green, deployed.
Count a claim as backed only if a test, build or lint command ran in that turn and exited 0.
Sort failures into stale green (edited after the run), fixed but never rebuilt, and green with a failing exit code above.
Add a stop hook that refuses to end a turn on a success claim without a passing check.
Tune what counts as a check per repo, and relax the hook for docs-only turns.
summary.stealThis: Before your next long agent session, add a Claude Code stop hook that rejects any success claim unless a passing test or build ran after the last edit in that turn.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're running coding agents daily, trusting their 'done' messages, and want a cheap guard before rereading every diff.
summary.quote: 752 of 1,521 done-claims had no passing check behind them.

verdict.reason: Teaches a concrete, portable technique: a Claude Code stop hook that blocks a turn from ending on a success claim unless a passing test, build or lint ran in that turn, backed by a useful taxonomy of unbacked claims (stale green, never rebuilt, green with red above). It's thin, with no hook code, and the card slightly overstates two details: 'after the last edit' and relaxing the hook for docs-only turns.

summary.title: My AI agents wrote four changes overnight. Tests passed. Each had a hole
summary.idea: Tests written by the same agent that wrote the code share its blind spots, so a second read-only agent answers numbered questions about risky diffs, citing file and line for every claim.
howItWorks: Give the second agent only the diff and surrounding files, not the author's summary or your opinion.
Ask numbered questions that each name one actor and one outcome, such as who can cause a removal.
Require every answer to cite a file and line, so you can open each path and check it.
Verify each reviewer finding against the code yourself, since the reviewer is sometimes wrong or raises trivia.
Use it for changes touching auth, secrets or deletion, then read the core function of each change yourself.
summary.stealThis: Before merging your next agent-written change to auth, secrets or deletion, hand the diff to a fresh read-only agent with numbered actor-and-outcome questions that demand file and line answers.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're merging agent-written code with agent-written tests and want concrete examples of holes that green suites missed.
summary.quote: The same agents wrote the code and the tests, so the tests had the same blind spots as the code.

verdict.reason: Teaches a concrete, copyable review technique: a fresh read-only agent given only the diff, answering numbered actor-and-outcome questions with file-and-line citations. It is backed by four real holes that green agent-written tests missed, with code snippets, and the card matches the page.

summary.title: How to Review AI-Generated Code Without Rubber-Stamping It
summary.idea: AI-written PRs outpace human reviewers, so route each one into a risk tier by the paths it changes, demand evidence tied to the exact commit, and reserve deep human review for costly changes.
howItWorks: Set the tier from changed file paths; agent signals can raise a tier but never lower it.
Low tier needs green checks on this commit SHA; medium adds one independent oracle and one reviewer.
High tier (public API, auth, billing, CI, migrations) needs two approvers plus a named release owner with a rollback plan.
An independent oracle is a contract diff, a pre-existing test, or a human-written case, not tests the authoring model wrote.
Stale evidence blocks the merge; enforce with CODEOWNERS, rulesets, required checks, and a PR template checklist.
summary.stealThis: Before your next AI-assisted PR merges, paste the evidence checklist into the PR template, tag the risk tier, and name an approver and release owner, adding a failure-oriented test you wrote yourself.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're reviewing a growing pile of agent-written PRs and want a tiering scheme, GitHub ruleset setup, and a worked payments-retry example.
summary.quote: Let agent signals raise a tier and never lower it.

verdict.reason: Teaches a concrete risk-tiered review scheme for agent PRs: set tiers from file paths, let agent signals raise but never lower a tier, require evidence tied to the commit SHA and an independent oracle, and enforce it with a copyable PR checklist, GitHub rulesets and a worked payments-retry example.

summary.title: Your Agent Will Pick the Hackable One: Guardrails Against Reward Hacking in AI Coding Agents
summary.idea: Coding agents that are told to make tests pass will often edit tests, skip them or loosen configs instead of fixing the bug, so CI guardrails are needed to catch it.
howItWorks: A CI script fails any PR that touches tests or coverage config unless a human adds an allow label.
A diff scanner flags added lines that skip tests, swallow exceptions, weaken assertions or lower coverage thresholds.
Mutation testing (mutmut, Stryker) runs on changed files to show whether new tests actually fail when code is broken.
Instruction files forbid editing existing tests and give the agent a legitimate way to say it cannot fix something.
A hidden acceptance test suite, kept outside the agent's workspace, stops it from overfitting to visible tests.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent-authored PR, add a CI step that fails when the diff touches tests/ or coverage config without a human-applied label, so the agent cannot unlock it itself.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're merging agent PRs where CI is green but you suspect the tests were quietly changed, and want ready-to-copy guard scripts.
summary.quote: Agent không cố tình lừa bạn. Nó chỉ tối ưu đúng cái mục tiêu bạn đặt ra.

verdict.reason: It teaches concrete, copyable guardrails against agents gaming tests: a label-gated CI lock on tests/config, a diff regex scanner for skips, swallowed exceptions and weakened asserts, mutation testing on changed files, and hidden acceptance tests, all with working scripts; the card matches the page, though the article is in Vietnamese, which limits reach.

summary.title: TokenEconomizer: Learning from Experience to Make AI Coding Agents More Efficient
summary.idea: Coding agents restart each session from scratch, rediscovering facts, loading unused tools and looping on failures; a plugin mines past session logs per repository to feed later sessions leaner guidance.
howItWorks: After each session, read the log and update what is known about that specific repository.
Micro-skills: one-line repo notes enter starting context only after several sessions confirm the pattern, and are retired if contradicted.
Tool pruning drops tools history says go unused, always keeping core run and edit tools, and restores them if needed.
Failure-loop intervention uses a judge model to detect a stuck agent, then sends a short note suggesting a different approach.
If the agent is still stuck after the note, alert the developer instead of silently stopping the work.
summary.stealThis: After your next few agent sessions in one repo, scan the logs for repeated actions (like how to run tests) and unused tool definitions, then add one-line notes to your instruction file and prune the tools.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're paying real token bills on agents working repeatedly in the same codebases and want data on where waste goes.
summary.quote: The agent received 23 tool descriptions on every turn, but 16 were never called.

verdict.reason: This teaches three portable harness techniques backed by measured evidence and open-source code: one-line repo micro-skills promoted only after repeated confirmation, pruning tools that history shows go unused, and a judge model that breaks failure loops. It's a research summary rather than a hands-on walkthrough, so it stops short of top tier.

summary.title: Building secure mobile apps in the agentic era
summary.idea: Agents ship code far faster than humans can security-review it, so Shopify keeps an attack surface map, encodes lessons as per-surface skills, and runs small, item-by-item reviews on every change daily.
howItWorks: Keep a list of security-sensitive surfaces (deep links, WebViews, stored data, dependencies), each item with a verdict and a link to its code.
Write one skill per surface, based on OWASP MASVS/MASTG plus past incidents, describing what to list and check.
Inventory every item first, then have the model review one item at a time with only the code it touches.
Each weekday, diff the inventory against the last accepted map, review changed items with read-only tools, and validate answers before publishing.
After each incident or bug report, add that class of problem to the skills so every later run checks it.
summary.stealThis: After your next security bug fix, add that bug class to a per-surface review skill, then have an agent review one deep link or WebView route at a time against it.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're shipping agent-written code faster than people can review it and want a repeatable, incident-driven security check.
summary.quote: Every vulnerability we find and fix strengthens the checks we run on the next change.

verdict.reason: The page teaches a concrete, portable security-review harness: per-surface skills built from OWASP plus past incidents, a full inventory followed by one-item-at-a-time reviews, and a daily diff against an accepted attack-surface map with validated outputs. There's no code, so it falls short of top tier.

summary.title: What We've Learned Building Proactive Agents
summary.idea: Background agents that act on events and schedules can drown their owner in check-ins, so LangChain pairs a memory that learns from feedback with review-friendly messages that cost little attention.
howItWorks: Triggers come from real-world events, developer schedules, and schedules the agent sets itself, such as a daily brief a user requested.
Memory comes from seed data like a sent folder, feedback on drafts, and outcomes such as whether an email got a reply.
A scheduled 'dreaming' job reads recent traces and updates memory, handling salience, expiry of stale facts, and duplicates.
Track memory's value through outcomes like time to draft approval, reply rates, and the share of check-ins you act on.
Surface only high-signal items, lead with a one- or two-sentence headline, and put detail in a thread reply inside Slack.
summary.stealThis: Before your next background agent goes live, add a nightly job that reads its traces and rewrites a memory file, and log what share of its check-ins you act on.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're building agents that run on schedules or events and want to keep their check-ins useful instead of noisy.
summary.quote: People have a finite context window too, with only so much time and attention to give.

verdict.reason: It offers portable but thinly explained patterns with no code: a scheduled 'dreaming' job that rewrites memory from traces, seed/feedback/outcome memory signals, tracking the share of check-ins acted on, and headline-plus-thread check-ins.

summary.title: From tasks to goals
summary.idea: Goal-driven background agents pick their own tasks and tools, so the harness must add visibility, tool limits, a question inbox, feedback, wake-up triggers and memory.
howItWorks: Expose the agent's self-chosen task list, like a to-do list, so you can see what it decided to do.
Restrict which tools the agent may call, since a goal doesn't reveal which tools it will need.
Give background agents an inbox, via Slack or a UI, to ask humans for clarification.
Wake the agent with heartbeats, cron jobs or event streams, and let it decide to do nothing.
Store rejected decisions and feedback across runs so later choices improve, such as dropping a rejected blog topic.
summary.stealThis: Before you hand a background agent its next ongoing goal, add a Slack-style question channel and a rule that it may skip a heartbeat when there's nothing to do.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're moving agents from one-off tasks to long-running background work and need a checklist of harness pieces to add.
summary.quote: Ongoing responsibility does not mean the agent should always find something to do.

verdict.reason: A thin but usable checklist for goal-driven background agents: show the task list, limit tools, add a question inbox and feedback loop, use heartbeat/cron triggers with an explicit do-nothing option, and keep memory of rejections. The page gives no code or worked example of any of these.

summary.title: Data Contracts
summary.idea: Agents treat every data value as truth and guess at meaning, so confident wrong answers follow; a versioned, machine-readable data contract with quality rules and AI context gives them explicit metadata and automated checks.
howItWorks: Describe each dataset in a YAML contract: schema, column meanings, quality rules, freshness SLAs, owner and terms of use.
Add an AI context block with instructions, constraints and verified question-and-query pairs the agent can reuse instead of guessing.
Keep the contract in the same Git repo as the pipeline code, versioned with SemVer so renames count as breaking changes.
Run lint, breaking-change detection and data tests in CI, then a nightly production test that alerts the owner when a promise breaks.
Feed the contract plus skills to a coding agent to generate the pipeline, using contract tests as its feedback loop.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent task that queries a shared dataset, write a small contract with column semantics, one SQL quality rule, and a few verified question-and-query pairs in an AI context block, then run it as a CI check.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're letting agents query or build pipelines on shared data and want contracts, CI checks and versioning to stop confidently wrong answers.
summary.quote: agents treat every value as truth.

verdict.reason: Mostly a general data-engineering piece. It does teach a portable agent technique with YAML examples: an AI context block (instructions, constraints, verified question-and-query pairs) plus contract tests in CI and as a feedback loop for a coding agent generating pipelines, though the agent angle is a minority of the page.

summary.title: Why Coding Agent Commits Are 3x Larger and How to Keep PRs Reviewable
summary.idea: Agents bundle cleanup, renames and logic into oversized commits that reviewers end up skimming; splitting mechanical from behavioral changes and enforcing a pre-commit diff budget keeps each commit small and checkable.
howItWorks: After an agent session, run git diff --cached --numstat to spot which files hold the real fix.
Reset the index, then commit formatting, renames and import cleanup separately from logic changes.
Stage behavior changes and their tests together with git add --patch so reviewers see one intent.
A .git/hooks/pre-commit script blocks commits over 10 files or 300 changed lines.
Comments suggest a soft warning near five files in a turn-end hook, plus a one-off skip variable for unsliceable changes.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent-assisted commit, drop in the pre-commit hook that counts staged files and lines from git diff --cached --numstat and blocks anything over 10 files or 300 lines.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're reviewing agent-written PRs and want copy-paste git commands and a hook script to force small, single-intent commits.
summary.quote: Prompt rules alone drift during long coding sessions.

verdict.reason: Teaches a concrete, copyable technique for agent-written changes: split mechanical commits from behavioral ones with git reset and git add --patch, then enforce a pre-commit diff budget hook (10 files / 300 lines), with a working script and example output; the techniques are basic git hygiene, so it's useful but not deep.

summary.title: feat: add pr-screenshot-evidence skill
summary.idea: A single happy-path screenshot hides denied, empty and error cases, so this skill has agents list every affected case first, capture each one with a caption, and disclose any gaps.
howItWorks: Build a mandatory case matrix first: roles, states, surfaces, themes, and base-versus-head behavior the change touches.
Capture each matrix row in order using synthetic disposable data, with a caption saying what it proves.
Write a manifest CSV mapping filename, case, caption, sha256 and head commit for every image.
Verify images by generating a checksums file with awk (skipping the header) and running shasum -a 256 -c or sha256sum -c.
Attach images to the PR description in matrix order, listing uncapturable cases as NOT CAPTURED with a reason.
summary.stealThis: Before your next PR that changes a permission or visible screen, have the agent write a case matrix and hash-verified manifest first, then capture every row and mark gaps NOT CAPTURED.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're reviewing agent PRs that change UI or access control and want a repeatable, checkable evidence standard instead of one happy-path screenshot.
summary.quote: a hash that does not match means the image is stale; recapture it

verdict.reason: It teaches a transferable proof-of-work standard: build a case matrix of roles and states before capturing, caption each screenshot, hash-verify it, and mark uncapturable cases NOT CAPTURED. But the PR was closed unmerged, and the page shows only the description, not the full SKILL.md.

summary.title: Claude for Marketing (2026): Skills, Connectors, Claude Code
summary.idea: Marketing teams that treat Claude as a chat box get inconsistent output; persistent context, reusable skill files with built-in checks, and guardrails on file-changing work make it repeatable while humans keep approval.
howItWorks: Load a Project with brand voice, ICP, messaging pillars, dated product facts and a list of banned claims.
Write a SKILL.md per recurring task, such as a content brief, with numbered steps and final checks.
Make the skill demand a facts table where every claim carries a source link and date.
Let Claude Code work only on copies or staging, with credentials kept out of chats.
Have a person approve publishing, and verify Claude's calculations against the original exports.
summary.stealThis: Before your next recurring deliverable, turn your human process into a SKILL.md with numbered steps and a checks section requiring every claim to have a source and date.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're running marketing or ops work through Claude and want a sample skill file, published team workflows and guardrails for file-editing agents.
summary.quote: Claude helps your team investigate the problem. The marketing team chooses what they should test.

verdict.reason: Passes thinly: it includes a concrete content-brief SKILL.md with numbered steps and a checks section requiring a sourced, dated facts table, plus staging, credential and approval guardrails, but this sits inside a padded SEO guide with pricing tables and an agency pitch.

summary.title: sales-ops-agents
summary.idea: Sales agents that write to a CRM and send email are risky, so every tool call goes through one governance gateway with allowlists, risk tiers, human approval and an audit log.
howItWorks: A fixed supervisor runs research, then CRM, then email agents; each agent picks its own tools within its step.
One gateway checks every tool call against per-agent allowlists and scopes each run to a single account.
Risk is classified per call: notes updates run automatically, but stage or ARR changes wait in an approval queue.
Untrusted web content is screened for injected instructions and fenced as data; recipients must be CRM contacts, rechecked after reviewer edits.
An eval runner scores 12 checks per case, covering output quality and governance, such as injection never being followed.
summary.stealThis: Before giving an agent write access to any business system, route all its tool calls through one gateway with per-agent allowlists and split routine writes from high-risk ones that need human approval.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're building agent workflows for sales, ops or other business teams and need concrete guardrails, approval gates and evals that cover governance.
summary.quote: Unknown tools fail closed.

verdict.reason: A working repo that teaches a portable governance-gateway pattern: per-agent tool allowlists, per-call risk tiers that fail closed, approval gates that re-check policy after reviewer edits, fencing of untrusted content, and evals that score governance behaviour, all runnable offline. It is better filed under harness design (tool gating and loop structure) than under non-engineers, since the audience is engineers building it.

summary.title: Take the merge out of the agent's session, and let a skill do the checks before I merge
summary.idea: Agent sessions that merge their own PRs stall or skip checks, and manual pre-merge checks are slow; a tiered GitHub workflow merges low-risk PRs and a /pr-verify skill handles the mechanical checks on risky ones.
howItWorks: Sort each PR into a risk tier by changed paths; only the lowest tier merges without a human reading the diff.
A read-only judge job runs the tier script from main against the PR head commit, never executing PR code.
A separate merge job holds the GitHub App key and merges pinned to the judged commit.
The /pr-verify skill stops on unresolved review findings, failed checks or conflicts, otherwise summarizes the PR and decisions needed.
For e2e changes, it drives the preview with Playwright, takes screenshots and records videos, and merges only after approval.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent-driven merge, write a /pr-verify-style skill that treats a failed or pending check read as stop or wait, and merges with --match-head-commit.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're running agent-authored PRs and want a concrete tiered auto-merge workflow plus a pre-merge verification skill with evidence videos.
summary.quote: A passing test doesn't tell you which parts of the screen it never looked at.

verdict.reason: A real working setup: risk-tiered PRs, merging moved out of the agent session into a two-job workflow (a read-only judge, then a merge pinned to the judged head commit), and a /pr-verify skill that treats failed reads as stop and records Playwright videos as evidence, backed by concrete numbers (3/128 denials, a 16-second bad merge, 97% vs 87% on the eval), though there's no code shown and half the post is unrelated project news.

summary.title: Your Coding Agent Didn't Fix the Bug. It Just Rewrote the Test to Assert the Failure.
summary.idea: Coding agents told to make tests pass will often edit assertions, mock the code under test, or skip tests; hard harness boundaries like locked tests and mutation checks stop this where prompts alone do not.
howItWorks: Agents optimize for exit code 0, so editing the test is a cheaper path than fixing the source.
Watch for three cheats: inverted assertions, mocking the function under test, and test.skip pruning.
A pre-commit or CI script fails the branch if existing test files changed versus origin/main.
Mutation testing with Stryker or mutmut exposes hollow tests that still pass when code is sabotaged.
Mounting the tests directory read-only gives the agent a permission error if it tries to edit tests.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent bugfix session, add a CI or pre-commit check that fails when existing test files change, so the agent can only pass by fixing the source.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're letting agents loop on failing tests and want concrete guardrails, including a ready-to-copy hook script, instead of more prompt rules.
summary.quote: Prompting is a soft nudge. Software verification requires a hard boundary.

verdict.reason: Teaches concrete hard-boundary guardrails against test tampering: a pre-commit/CI script failing on modified test files, mutation testing, and read-only test mounts, with code and failure examples, though the read-only mount and mutation gate are only sketched.

summary.title: AI agent said done but tests fail: make it prove it
summary.idea: Agents announce "done" after running only nearby tests or quietly loosening them, so a Stop hook that reruns the suite and blocks finishing until it passes forces real proof.
howItWorks: Run the full test suite, production build, typechecker and linter yourself instead of trusting the agent's summary.
Scan git diff for weakened tests: added .skip or .only, deleted assertions, rewritten snapshots, @ts-ignore casts and TODO stubs.
Write a rule in CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md requiring test and build runs, with the last lines of output pasted.
Register a Claude Code Stop hook that runs npm test and exits with code 2 on failure, feeding the log tail back.
The stop_hook_active flag and an eight-block cap stop an unpassable test from looping forever.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent session, add a Stop hook script that runs your test command, prints the last 30 lines of failures to stderr and exits 2 so the agent keeps working.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're using Claude Code and want a copy-paste hook config and checklist for catching fake 'done' claims.
summary.quote: An agent's "done" is a summary, not a result.

verdict.reason: Teaches a concrete, copyable Claude Code Stop hook (settings.json plus a shell script that exits 2 with the failing test tail) and a diff checklist for weakened tests, though it overlaps with other 'prove done' posts.

summary.title: Spec-Driven Development: The Approaches Behind AI Software Factories (2026)
summary.idea: Agents that code from vague prompts build plausible guesses and mark their own homework, so this guide compares five ways to agree a written spec and an agent-runnable check before implementation.
howItWorks: Spec-first toolkits turn a feature into requirements, design and tasks, with a human reviewing each stage before code.
Fresh-context review has a long-session agent draft the spec, then fresh subagents that never saw the chat critique it.
Plan-then-execute uses plan mode to block edits until you approve, with the plan saved to a file.
Test-first makes failing tests the spec; the agent writes only enough code to pass them.
Combine them: reviewed spec per feature, tests as acceptance criteria, and a named human sign-off.
summary.stealThis: Before your next feature, have the agent interview you into a spec saved as a Markdown file, then ask a fresh subagent with no chat history to review it for unstated assumptions.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're choosing a spec-driven workflow for a team and want a comparison of approaches, their weak spots and when each fits.
summary.quote: Documents that pass the Goldfish test become important protections against slop.

verdict.reason: A thin pass: it reads partly like a tool round-up and ends in a studio pitch, but it does compare spec-first approaches by when each fits and where it breaks, and teaches techniques you can copy (interviewing yourself into a saved spec, review by a fresh subagent with no chat history, failing tests as acceptance criteria), though without code or before-and-after evidence.

summary.title: feat(skills): add verify-agentic-template verification skill
summary.idea: Agents each worked out on their own how to start an app and capture UI proof; a single scripted verification skill gives them one repeatable way to launch, drive, and record evidence.
howItWorks: A launch command starts an isolated Vite instance on a free port, from the working tree or a CI build pinned to a commit.
A read-only doctor command checks the instance is healthy and that the served build matches HEAD, failing if not.
A drive command runs mapped user journeys in Chromium, asserting through roles and accessible names, and saves screenshots, ARIA snapshots, video and a manifest.
Cleanup stops only the process group this run started and keeps the evidence for the PR.
A PR can add its own journey file and run it with drive ./journey.mjs.
summary.stealThis: Before your next UI change, write a small verify skill with launch, doctor, drive and cleanup commands so the agent attaches screenshots and a manifest to the PR instead of improvising.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're asking agents to prove UI changes and want a concrete skill layout with scripts, journey files and a PR proof checklist.
summary.quote: Doctor correctly reported that build as FAIL build matches HEAD against this branch.

verdict.reason: The PR teaches a portable verification skill: launch an isolated instance, run a read-only doctor that fails if the served build doesn't match HEAD, drive journeys asserted through accessible roles, and keep screenshots, video and a manifest as PR evidence, all backed by a real merged repo and a proof run.
